What the award record shows

PUBLIC RECORD · DEMAND SIGNALS
Three readings drawn straight from the public award record: how this contractor's largest jobs compare to its recent norm, how concentrated its work is by agency, and how often it has appeared as a winner. They describe what the City has hired the firm to do. They are not a credit opinion, a bonding judgment, or a prequalification, and nothing here scores or ranks the contractor.

Registered and paid

CHECKBOOK NYC · USD
Three different measures of this firm's City work, shown side by side and never added together. The award-notice value is the amount stated when a contract is awarded. Registered is the contract value the Comptroller has registered. Paid to date is how much the City has actually disbursed against those registered contracts. Each answers a different question, and the gaps between them are normal.

MTA & State public work

DATA.NY.GOV · USD
Public construction work this firm has done for the MTA and New York State, named in the State's open-data record. This is a separate ledger from the City figures above and is never added to them. Heavy-civil firms whose New York work runs through the authorities can read low or empty in the City and Checkbook views precisely because their work shows up here instead.

Methodology & definitions

SERIES NOTES

How vendor totals are grouped

Figures on this page come from the New York City Record Recent Contract Awards dataset (NYC Open Data qyyg-4tf5), limited to awards in Construction categories. Many firms appear under several spellings of their name, and a single firm group can file under more than one legal entity. Where we can confirm by hand that several names belong to the same firm, we group them under one parent total and list every underlying name and its amount, so nothing is hidden. Grouping is a fixed, verified list of name variants, not automated name-matching or any statistical guess. We group only on a distinctive shared identifier or an unmistakable spelling variation of the same company; when a connection is uncertain, we leave the names separate. Each amount is the value stated in the award notice, which is a floor rather than a running total of work performed or paid, so a group's total is a lower bound. The City Record covers City-agency awards only; MTA and New York State construction work is shown separately in the MTA & State panel below, drawn from the State's own named-vendor data. The School Construction Authority and the Port Authority remain out of scope for naming a contractor, because those datasets carry no vendor field.

Where registered and paid come from

The award-notice figure is queried live from the City Record on each load. The registered and paid figures come from Checkbook NYC, the Comptroller's system of record, which a browser cannot call directly: it allows no cross-origin request and returns a paged XML feed. So an automated job fetches and normalizes it server-side every night and writes a compact static file this page reads. That job reconciles each Checkbook vendor name to the same parent groups used here, through the same normName() normalization the award record uses, so the three measures line up against one contractor. A group with no exact name match after normalization shows no Checkbook figure rather than a guess.

MTA & State public work

The MTA and State figures come from New York State open data on data.ny.gov: MTA Procurements (twsw-2mqa) and the State University Construction Fund contracts (cfjm-ii27), both limited to the Design and Construction/Maintenance procurement type. These datasets name the awarded contractor, so they close the contractor-naming gap that City sources leave on authority work. They are reported through the Public Authorities Reporting Information System, which re-reports every active contract each fiscal year with a growing cumulative spend, so the figures here are deduplicated to one record per contract at its latest fiscal-year report; summing the raw rows would multi-count. These are a separate ledger from the City and Checkbook figures and are never added to them, because they sit on different books. A firm with no exact name match after normalization shows nothing here rather than a guess.

The Concrete Index is an independent personal project built on public data. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or speaking for any employer, and nothing here is any employer's assessment of any named company.

Winners only

Award notices name the winning contractor only, so this shows who was awarded work, not who else bid. The losing bidders on a given solicitation are not in this record.

A note for credit work

This is the public demand-side view of a contractor: what the City has hired it to do. It says nothing about costs, margins, bonding capacity, or performance. Treat it as one input alongside financials, not a substitute for them.
